Canadian Camping 




TO OOR COUNStUORS! 


If you look in the dictionary you will 
see that the meaning of the word 
counsellor is: “one who helps and 
guides by word and deed.” Every staff 
member at camp must be sure that his 


words and actions are of good report 
so that our campers may look up to each 
one of us, sure in his heart that our 
words are worth listening to and that 
our actions are worth following. 


1. Your dress and appearance are important 

2. Your manner of speaking to everyone in camp will be listened 
to and copied. Keep it interesting and free from argument and nasty 
words. 

3. The way you work with your fellow counsellors is of great 
interest to campers. This could set the pattern for the campers* 
relations one to another. 

4. Your table manners—are they worth copying? 

5. Your relation to prayer, God and His Church—they must inspire 
and help your campers feel close to God. 

6. Your chit-chat in a room full of campers about your dates and 
fun—should it all be heard by kids? If so, fine. 

7. Is getting out of bed a hard job? Do children annoy you early 
in the morning? If the answer is yes to either of these questions, 
think seriously about being or continuing to be a counsellor. 

8. Do you put your own things away? Are they taken good care 
of? I’m sure if the campers were asked, they could tell. 

9. Are you a good sport? Is the winning more important than the 
game? 

10. Gan you take children for a long period of time and keep them 
happy and interested? 

11. Your day off is important to both the campers and yourself. 
Use it wisely. 


Your position as a counsellor is a 
very important one. It carries with it 
a great deal of responsibility of action 
and deed. It is not enough to be able 
to do a thing well, the important thing 
is, how is it done? What have you and 
the campers learned by doing it? 

Each minute in our lives is a learning 
process and our goal is to learn those 
things which are going to make our 
lives useful and happy. A camp has one 
primary duty and that is to see that 


every camper learns to become a better 
person by being at camp. 

Camping can be a truly great educa¬ 
tional experience in a child’s life. Our 
camp should be dedicated to the ideal 
that people come to know, and respect 
one another by living and working 
together. 

—E. Hilton Chaloner, Director, 

St. George’s Episcopal Church Camps 
Saugerties, N.Y. 


Toronto, Canada, June , 1955 


9 


How Are You Off 
For Leadership ? 


Excerpts from an address given by 
Rev. Wilbur Howard , Associate Edi¬ 
tor, Sunday School Publications, 
United Church of Canada, at the 
1955 Ontario Camping Conference. 


Camping trends may come and 
camping trends may go but ’leadership 
is the continuing factor. 

Camping , b as gone through many 
stages. Here are some of the stages 
that we might recognize: 

1. The Wild and Woolly Stage 

This was the early day of camping. 
It was the time of “Throw ’em in the 
drink” . . . Morning jerks . . . Blow 
that whistle! . . . Ring that bell! . . . 
Sleeping on grassblade and ground 
sheet. ... 

2. The Lean Towards Hygiene 

Then the pendulum took a swing. 
We concerned ourselves about health 
and safety . . . water safety . . . elation 
over sanitation . . . the chlorine dip for 
dishes. . . . And, of course, all this took 
more and better leadership. 

3. Throw Back or Go Back 

We realized that perhaps we were 
getting too civilized. So, it was back to 
the birds and bees . . . Nature boy stuff 
. . . Turn them loose with their native 
ingenuity and a hatchet. 


Now, I wonder what will our next 
trend be? My suggestion is that we 
are ready for a period when we capi¬ 
talize on this phrase, “Relax and 
Think.” 

But, we have noted, that through¬ 
out the many stages of camping the 
one continuing factor has been 
leadership. 


What Loadernhip 
do You Need? 

You’ll know the answer to that bet¬ 
ter than I will. It depends partly upon 
your philosophy of camping, your 
goals and objectives. 

Your camp leadership might include 
the following: 

1. Single Persons and Married 
Couples. How about that? How about 
having a married couple as cabin 


10 


Canadian Camping 



leaders? We’re pretty serious, aren’t 
we, about the influence of parents and 
the home? 

2. Old and Young. Iiovv old? You 
might have at least one grandfather 
or grandmother in spite of the saying: 
“Only the young die good.” Our boys 
and girls had better learn how to relate 
to older people because there will be 
plenty of them in the Canada of the 
future. Older people have some con¬ 
tributions to make that younger leaders 
would not be able to make. A grand¬ 
mother, for instance, can apply an 
emotional mustard plaster. Older 
people have a steadying wisdom and 
understanding that seem to undergird 
a camp or a problem with strength. 
How young should your leaders be? 
Perhaps we should investigate the idea 
of having leaders the same age as the 
campers. But aside from this adven¬ 
ture in daring experiment, they should 
be mature persons 18 years of age and 
older. 

3. Two or Three Different Races. 
If we’re really serious about establish¬ 
ing better relationships with people of 
other nationalities and races, then we 
should be practical about it and get 
other races and nationalities into our 
camps. We do not need to worry too 
much about attitudes when boys and 
girls have had a close-in camping ex¬ 
perience with people who represent 
countries and races different from 
theirs. 

4. Some Home-grown, Some Im¬ 
ports. You should have some leaders 
who have come up through your camps 
and know your traditions and are at 
home on your camp site. But you 
should not have all your leaders of 
this kind. If they are all home-grown, 
then your leadership tends to be in- 
grown. You need some imports. I 
heard recently that they were con- 



Counselling at Camp Wooded'em 
for crippled children 


sidering holding the Grey Cup finals 
next year in the United States. It 
seems a shame to bring all those 
players up to Canada for the play-offs. 
Well, in our camp we need some im¬ 
ports—New blood that comes in and 
mixes with those of us who have been 
in the camping situation for a number 
of years and have kind of got used to its 
contours, both geographical and 
programme. 

All leaders, the cook, the mainten¬ 
ance man. the section leader, the unit 
head, the counsellor, all leaders should 
be trained in human relations. They 
should know what it means to get along 
with others (a) their fellow leaders, 
(b) the campers. They should know 
what it means to get along with others 
as individuals and how to work with 
groups. I was interested when I visited 
Youth House in New York (Youth 
House is a detention home for juvenile 
delinquents) to see that their policy

Nature 9 s 
Craft Shop 


Mrs. A. H. Stoddard, 

Divisional Commissioner, 
Province of Quebec , 

Canadian Girl Guides Association 


Mane 







off) 




Nature’s Craft Shop has an unlim¬ 
ited stock of goods for us if we will 
only use our eyes and a little bit of 
imagination. In these sketches are a 
few ideas to show how we can very 
easily use nature’s products for our 
handicrafts. 


For the head and beak of birds, a 
maple seed, with part of the wing cut 
off, is ideal. Orange pips and even 
apple pips can be the head and beak 
for smaller birds. 


Old Mother Hen and her Baby 
Chicks require a spruce cone for her 
body, an orange pip for her head, and 
one or two feathers as her tail. Study 
your orange and grape fruit pips and 
pick out the ones which look like baby 
chickens. Stick in two tiny twigs for 
legs. 


Cones . . . spruce, pine, alder, hem¬ 
lock . . . can all be used as bodies for 
birds, animals and dolls. The heads of 
the latter two can be acorns, oak apples 
or small chestnuts. Scales of a pine 
cone can be ears and tail, and small 
twigs make arms and legs.

Canadian Camping 



Beech nut cases which have not 
opened out too much, and have the 
stalk still on, make good bodies and 
necks of birds. A maple seed, again 
with part of the wing cut off, is the 
head and beak. Feathers or pine 
needles make the tail, and a twig for 
a leg . . . one leg is much easier to fix 
than two . . . and you can pretend that 
your bird has his other leg tucked up 
under him! Stick his one leg into a 
piece of bark. A few pine needles can 
be “grass” growing beside him. 


is vT 

Pf£LOAf 




A walnut shell, a small acorn or 
orange pip and four melon seeds make 
a realistic turtle. 



Orange and grapefruit pips can be 
made into little ducklings, with a grape 
pip for head and beak. Mama duck 
can be a peach stone with a hazel nut 
or orange pip for her head and beak. 
Mount them on a piece of bark. 

A small milkweed seed pod can also 
be Mama duck’s body, with an orange 
pip again as head and beak. 


A lovely swan is ready-made by 
Nature in a milkweed seed pod with 
the stem for its neck, and a maple seed 
(with part of the wing cut off) stuck 
on for head and beak. 


Acorns (without their “caps”) can 
be made into rabbits, squirrels, pen¬ 
guins, birds. Save your musk melon 
seeds for small ears and flappers and 
feet of penguins. 


Oak apples, which are a gall, not the 
fruit of the oak tree, are good material 
''for heads and bodies. Date stones can 
be legs, and watermelon seeds can be 
ears.

Peanuts are fun! Hold them up and 
see what kind of animals their shapes 
suggest to you. Citron, watermelon, 
musk melon and squash seeds make 
ears, tails, wings, beaks, legs, etc. 
Squash seeds cut in half make legs for 
this four-footed animal. 



Saw a few slices about to 1" 
thick, off different sized branches. Use 
the larger size circle for a body and 
the smaller one for a head, with, per¬ 
haps, prune stones for ears, small 
acorns for eyes and buttons, and chips 
of wood for feet. A coat of varnish will 
finish him off'. 


The only tools you require are a 
penknife, scissors, a small awl or pier¬ 
cer to make holes, some straight pins 
to help keep heads on, and a bottle or 
tube of glue . . . not too thin. Seccotine 
is good. 


Paint your birds and animals and 
dolls in bright colours if you like, with 
quick-drying enamels. A first coat of 
flat white paint allowed to dry before

Canadian Camping 




AMONG 

OURSELVES 



Taylor Statten, 


By J. H. Ebbs, M.D. 

Director , Health and Safety 
Taylor Statten Camps 


This year marks the Golden Anniver¬ 
sary in camping for Taylor Statten. In 
1905 when he became Boys’ Work Sec¬ 
retary of the Central Y.M.C.A. in To¬ 
ronto, he conducted his first boys’ 
camp at Lake Couchiching, marking 
the beginning of a career in camping 
which is still being carried on. Each 
successive year he has organized and 
conducted a camp with increasing en¬ 
thusiasm and with an ever-increasing 
experience, which he says deepens his 
appreciation of the tremendous values 
which come from the camping experi¬ 
ence of boys and girls. 

Taylor Statten has been for many 
years, a world figure in Y.M.C.A. boys’ 
work, first at Central Y.M.C.A. Toron¬ 
to, and later as Provincial and Cana¬ 
dian Boys’ Work Secretary. In 1921, 


he was appointed Secretary to the Na¬ 
tional Boys’ Work Board. During all 
of these years he was very interested 
in, and was responsible for at least 
52 camps conducted by the Y.M.C.A. 

In 1914 he originated and, with a 
group of other interested persons, set 
up the Canadian Standard Efficiency 
Training Programme for Tuxis boys 
and Trail Rangers, a movement which 
has undoubtedly affected the lives of 
thousands of boys and girls. 

In 1920 he conducted a leadership 
training camp for Tuxis boys’ leaders 
at Canoe Lake and the following year 
started Camp Ahmek for boys in Al¬ 
gonquin Park. In his first year as a 
private camp director with 30 boys, he 
established standards of camping which 
attracted many outstanding leaders 
and the camp grew steadily until it 
became necessary to establish it as five 
separate age group camps with one 
central organization. 

continued next page 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1955 


15 






In the early days of Camp Ahmek 
many famous names were associated 
with the Statten Camps, notably Ernest 
Thompson Seton, who introduced 
much of his Indian lore and wild-life 
legends to Canoe Lake. A nature 
museum is being created in his mem¬ 
ory in the original Seton cabin on the 
shores of Canoe Lake. Jack Miner’s 
annual visit stimulated an increasing 
interest in bird-life which was carried 
on for many years by Mr. and Mrs. 
Stuart Thompson. To these, and to a 
group of early leaders, such as Charles 
Hendry, Joseph McCulley, Hedley Di¬ 
mock, Alex Edmison, Ronald Perry 
and a host of others, Taylor Statten 
will give much credit for his great suc¬ 
cess. However, his contagious enthu¬ 
siasm and magnetic personality at¬ 
tracted the best in young people. Two 
men have been outstanding in their 
loyalty and service to the “Chief’— 
they are George Chubb, the business 
manager, and Pete Sauve, head chef, 
who have been with the Statten Camps 
since their inception in 1921. 

In 1924, under the directorship of 
Mrs. Taylor Statten, a girls’ camp was 
established on the same Lake in spite 
of warnings that co-educational camp¬ 
ing would ruin his original camping 
venture. Contrary to this, he built up 
a brother and sister type camp, pro¬ 
viding co-operative management with a 
maximum of efficiency, and a pro¬ 
gramme which could be controlled to 
the needs of various aged boys and 
girls. Camp Ahmek and Camp Wa- 
pomeo on Canoe Lake have been at¬ 
tended by thousands of boys and girls 
from throughout North America and 
other parts of the world, some now 
representing the third generation of 
Statten campers. 

In 1950 Taylor Statten, along with 
four other pioneer leaders in camping, 
was chosen to receive a special award 


from the American Camping Associa¬ 
tion for outstanding leadership. Quot¬ 
ing from the American magazine: 

“Taylor Statten, ably assisted by his 
wife, daughter Mrs. Harry Ebbs and 
son Dr. Taylor Statten, has made a 
lasting contribution to the camping 
field. Thousands of camp directors and 
camps have been influenced by his pio¬ 
neering achievements.” His leadership 
in the organized camping movement 
has been acknowledged by his election 
as the first President of the Canadian 
Camping Association and the only Ca¬ 
nadian to be elected President of the 
American Camping Association. 

Mr. Statten’s influence has also been 
felt in educational fields. In 1927 he 
becam° director of character education 
for Pickering College at the time that 
it was re-established. He continued in 
this until 1940 when he became presi¬ 
dent of the Metropolitan Board of the 
Y.M.C.A. and later took on the ardu¬ 
ous task of being secretary to the Met¬ 
ropolitan Board during the difficult war 
years. In the first World War he was 
director of the Sons of the Soil for 
the Canada Food Board from 1914- 
1918 and travelled with the troops in 
Europe carrying on part of the 
Y.M.C.A. programme. 

The first Canadian National Camp 
Training course was conducted under 
his patronage and the annual staff 
training programme each year is at¬ 
tended by more than two hundred 
counsellors and leaders. The camping 
world was stimulated more than twenty 
years ago by the publishing of “Camp¬ 
ing and Character”, a book which had 
its origin in Taylor Statten’s camp. 
His “Talks to Counsellors” is still in 
great demand by camp leaders. 

There has always been something of 
the “showman” in Taylor Statten, pos¬ 
sibly inherited from one of his circus 


16 


Canadian Camping 


ancestors, but year after year, lie ap¬ 
pears on “Circus Day” at camp in a 
new role—one time a ringmaster or a 
“Southern Colonel” and another time 
as Neptune or a Greek God—but al¬ 
ways with enthusiasm for the show 
which is to follow his official opening 
ceremony. Many of his “dreams” have 
not come true but so many have suc¬ 
ceeded, such as the building of a pirate 
ship, a log theatre and acquiring a full 
brass band, that those who know him 
well have learned to wait with expecta¬ 
tion for his next dream to come true. 
His desire to introduce something new 
each year resulted in 1929, in members 
of the Arts and Letters Club of To¬ 
ronto, arriving in camp with much 
fanfare disguised as English nobility. 
The “stunt” was being carried ofT very 
successfully until the son of one of the 
actors recognized his “Duke” father 
and gave the show away. The memory 
of campers and staff were long enough 
to make them highly suspicious the 


following year, when Lord and Lady 
Willingdon, the Governor General of 
Canada, visited the Camps. His Lord- 
ship was fortunate that he did not fol¬ 
low his bogus predecessors into the lake! 

The influence of Tom Thomson at 
Canoe Lake stimulated his interest in 
the Arts and has resulted in a long 
series of well-known artists finding an 
outlet for their talents in Algonquin 
Park. Music has been maintained on a 
high level owing to his insistence that 
the camp musicians be the best, with 
a desire to help young people appre¬ 
ciate good music. The Canoe Lake 
Theatre has been blessed with some 
inspiring directors starting with Roland 
Young and including Arthur 
Sutherland. 

In 1938 Mr. and Mrs. Statten jour¬ 
neyed to India where they officially 
opened Camp Tonakela near Madras. 

continued on next page 







Through his encouragement Mr. Wal¬ 
lace Forgie was persuaded to devote 
his life to the organization and direc¬ 
torship of this camp for underpriv¬ 
ileged boys and girls. The ever-widen¬ 
ing circle of campers in North America., 
who are now helping to support this 
venture, are helping democracy and 
our Western way of life by showing an¬ 
other side of the world the value of 
sharing. To hundreds of street boys 
and orphan 'd girls the camp provides 
a holiday with something of the North 
American styled camping experience. 
To hundreds of other young children it 
marks the life centre where they get 
their only real meal each day—in an 
area where drought has repeatedly 
caused a crop failure. Camp Tonakela, 
named from Mrs. Statten’s Indian 
name, is a fine outpost of democracy 
and a demonstration to the leaders of 
India of a fine camping programme 
originating in North America and sup¬ 


ported by its children. Needless to say 
it is a venture which Taylor Statten 
watches with justifiable pride. 

Many camp directors owe their in¬ 
terest and start in the camping field to 
the enthusiasm and generous leadership 
given by “Chief” Taylor Statten. It is 
also safe to say that thousands of 
former counsellors and campers have 
been influenced by their contact with 
him. It is hoped that Taylor Statten 
will be spared to enjoy many more 
years of enthusiastic leadership with 
his children and many long-time asso¬ 
ciates and admirers who gather on the 
shores of Canoe Lake in Algonquin 
Park.

SOME SUGGESTED 

TRAINING 

TECHNIQUES 


There is no group in camping to-day 
that would suggest seriously that we 
need not train our camp staffs. There 
are, however, differences of opinion 
about what we mean by training, and 
even more diversity around our train¬ 
ing objectives. 

As I observe the scene, most camps 
engage in some form of pre-camp train¬ 
ing, and let it go at that. 

From time to time groups in the 
Camping Association have tried to 
evaluate the effectiveness of pre-camp 
counsellor training. In most of the 
instances studied, the demonstrated re¬ 
sults of pre-camp counsellor training 
have been disappointing, to say the 
least, and yet we persist in relying 
upon it almost wholly for our training 
programmes. Looking at it realistical¬ 
ly, pre-camp training does serve many 
useful functions. For some camps it 
accomplishes the work necessary for 
opening camp, and in so doing helps 
the staff members to become familiar 
and comfortable with the camp en¬ 
vironment and equipment. It settles 
them into camp life. Even more im¬ 
portant. if well done, it fuses the staff 


Alan F. Klein, 

Associate Professor, 
School of Social Work, 
University of Toronto 


into a group and sets the atmosphere 
for loyalty and team spirit. Budget- 
wise camp directors must equate these 
results with the cost of a pre-camp 
week on site. It is expensive business. 
Some might find that these results can 
be obtained in a shorter period of time 
if designed differently or that it could 
be done by combining pre-camp in-the- 
city meetings with a pre-camp week¬ 
end on the site. 

We should be quite clear, however, 
that while the above mentioned results 
are part of over-all training objectives 
they are not the real training goals. 
The goals I have in mind are related 
to the manner in which a counsellor 
handles himself on the job. You may 
call this leadership training, or training 
in working with children. If these are 
our basic goals, pre-camp training is 
not the most effective method for 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1955 


19 



achieving them. It is for this reason 
that I venture to oppose the trend and 
suggest that we undertake to do what 
we can do well, and use our time and 
methods with more discrimination. By 
this I mean that we teach programme 
skills in pre-camp training because we 
can, and because counsellors need to 
have activity skills if they are to be 
effective. Leadership skill is of para¬ 
mount importance, to be sure, but 
without camp activity skill, the coun¬ 
sellor is operating in the dark without 
the slightest idea of how to turn the 
lights on. Some may go through the 
entire summer in this state. 

The art and skill of working with 
children is best learned and hence 
taught on the job. This can be accom¬ 
plished through supervision and train¬ 
ing sessions with small homogeneous 
groups of counsellors. Supervision is 
an educational process through which a 
person who knows more teaches some 
one who knows less on a face-to-face 
basis. The prime factor is that the 
learner be helped to solve his own 
problems as they arise on the job. 
Learning is achieved when the learner 
is active and is engaged in solving prob¬ 
lems that have meaning to him or to 
her. For this reason, on the job learn¬ 
ing is faster and more effective than 
pre-camp learning. 

We have said that supervision is one 
of the most effective methods of train¬ 
ing. However, here also, I must risk 
censure and go contrary to the trend. 
This method has not been successful 
in many camps because a long time 
back someone sold us on the unit 
system. Unit or section heads were 
to supervise the counsellors. The idea 
is sound administratively. Decentrali¬ 
zation has many advantages but in 
reality supervision is not one of them 
because most of us can not obtain 
unit heads who are qualified to super¬ 
vise, either because we can not afford 


them or because they do not exist. It 
is said that if you wish to teach a dog 
some tricks you must know more than 
the dog does. Many unit heads do not 
know substantially more than the coun¬ 
sellors do, nor are they more mature, 
and secondly, they do not know how to 
supervise, which is a specific training 
skill. Consequently, we adopted an 
administrative structure and have re¬ 
lied upon it in many settings in spite 
of the fact that we have not been able 
to secure personnel appropriate to the 
structure to make it run at a high level 
of efficiency from a training point of 
view. I think I would prefer to employ 
one senior supervisor, charged with 
the responsibility of staff training, keep 
the decentralized plan by using a senior 
counsellor as my unit co-ordinator, and 
give up the idea of unit heads super¬ 
vising staff. 

In the last few years some new ideas 
have been developed in training and 
have proven themselves in industry and 
adult education. They might be used 
in pre-camp training or during the 
camp season. Those that I will , men¬ 
tion all depend upon a few fundamen¬ 
tal training principles: 

1. Only the counsellor can change 
his own performance. He must, 
therefore, be involved actively in the 
training process. 

2. Adults learn more readily 
through problem-solving exercises. 

3. Learning is accelerated if the 
problems discussed are significant to 
the learner. 

4. Aimless discussion is frustrating. 
There must be guidance and direc¬ 
tion by the trainer. 

5. Human relations skills require 
insight into one’s own way of 
working. 


20 


Canadian Camping 



6. The learners must want to learn 
and change. 

7. All learning is accompanied by 
resistance to learning which is in¬ 
tensified by threat or fear. 

8. Effective learning requires the 
support of a small friendly group of 
colleagues. 

These principles imply that all our 
personnel are committed to a common 
goal, and that the goal is made explicit. 
They imply also that the staff members 
experience satisfaction of their own 
personal needs. That means good in¬ 
terpersonal relationships; status given 
for doing a good job with campers and 
not for looks, apple polishing, athletic 
skill and so on; an atmosphere condu¬ 
cive to learning, with rewards based 
upon satisfaction from doing a good 
job accompanied by encouragement 
and praise; and an opportunity for 
shared leadership in a democratic 
setting. 

To summarize, then, the principles of 
all such training require that the 
learner have access to ideas, attitude 
and modes of behavior alternative to 
the ones he possesses; there must be a 
setting in which he can examine and 
test new ways; and he needs support 
and social success in experimenting 
with new forms of behavior before he 
can adopt them as his own. 

To clarify terms and concepts let us 
observe that training connotes “how to 
do a job” while education means some¬ 
thing broader. Here we are talking 
about training counsellors for a job. 

While we are clarifying, let us settle 
another question. Do our words so far 
mean that one may never lecture to 
counsellors? They do not. When the 
content consists of facts, procedures, 
and non-debatable material it can be 


given as a lecture or in a written man¬ 
ual. It is more useful and acceptable 
and therefore learned more quickly 
when the learner wants and needs the 
information, but we are not throwing 
the “telling** method out completely. 

The methods that follow will be de¬ 
scribed very briefly since each could be 
profitably the subject of an article by 
itself . 

Role Playing 

This is a training method that is 
both powerful and effective. In it the 
learning situation is enacted and meth¬ 
ods of handling oneself in the situation 
are tried and evaluated and then the 
new insights are tested. It has been 
abused by charlatans who have thought 
that all there was to it was to put on 
a dramatic skit. In fact, it is a sensi¬ 
tive training tool and should be studied 
before attempting to use it. It is ad¬ 
mirably suited to camp training. 

Case Study 

In this method a detailed narrative 
of a situation is given. The whole case 
is described. The trainees are asked to 
analyze what happened, to explain the 
behaviour of the campers, to critically 
examine the work of the counsellor and 
to suggest alternate ways of approach¬ 
ing the problem. 

The case might present a problem 
without revealing the counsellor’s ac¬ 
tion and the trainees may be asked 
what they would do. Alternate sug¬ 
gestions are examined and conse¬ 
quences explored. In this method, 
principles must be drawn from the 
discussion. Camp policy, procedures 
and routines can be taught at the same 
time from the same case. The cases 
are written from your own camp rec¬ 
ords and experiences. 

continued on page 23 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1955 


21

Canadian Camping 





continued from page 21 

The Incident Method 

In this method instead of giving a 
complete case, one sentence describing 
an incident is given. For example, 
“When the cabin group left for the 
council ring Joel refused to go, saying 
that he was tired.” The trainees must 
ask questions of the person who knows 
the full story. This might be a more 
experienced counsellor. The value of 
this method is that it helps the trainees 
to develop a questioning approach to 
situations, they learn what questions to 
ask and what to look for, and they get 
the information they want to know and 
not what we want to tell them. When 
they try to solve the problem they may 
find that they have not learned enough 
facts. This develops motivation to 
learn more. 

The trainee is stimulated to try to get 
his bearings in the situation. He must 
get the facts and then sort out the key 
facts. He must determine what the 
question is in the incident. 

After many questions have been 
asked and facts gleaned, the trainees 
are encouraged to summarize the situa¬ 
tion. Then every one is asked to write 
what he believes to be the real ques¬ 
tion, a solution and his reasons, in ten 
minutes. This prevents many from sit¬ 
ting back letting a few do the thinking 
and work. 

We then are ready to discuss. What 
are the possible decisions; what prin¬ 
ciples are involved? We examine all 
the actions, and consequences. How 
might the incident have been pre¬ 
vented ? What is a good working 
hypothesis ? 

The Observation Method 

Here I shall describe briefly a fas¬ 
cinating research project conducted by 
Dick McDonald in which he demon¬ 


strated conclusively that counsellor skill 
and behaviour could be improved 
greatly in a short time. Mr. McDonald 
worked with four counsellors during a 
camp season in a well known camp. 

1. The counsellors in discussion 
agreed upon the qualities a counsel¬ 
lor should have and manifest. 

2. They devised a form to use when 
observing a counsellor. 

3. They observed each other on the 
job, and in discussion revised the 
form. 

4. Three and the trainee observed 
the fourth, and all discussed what 
they saw and how it might be im¬ 
proved. This was done until each 
had been observed at least once. 

5. Four observed the trainer work 
with a group. This was discussed 
and analyzed. 

6. Each asked to be observed 
around a situation that was a prob¬ 
lem to him and after observations, 
possible solutions were discussed and 
the new ideas tried in later sessions 
with the campers. 

Those interested in training will find 
reading this project very rewarding. 
The principles established are appli¬ 
cable universally. 

Improved staff means improved per¬ 
formance, and better camping. Camp 
management has not kept up with the 
trend in other enterprises to improve 
and increase personnel training. It is 
good business and pays many different 
kinds of dividends. 

Source Material: 

It’s Wise to Supervise—Klein and 
Haladner. Canadian Camping Assn. 

Role Playing in Action Argyris—New 
York State School of Industrial and 
Labour Relations—Cornell University. 

Adult Leadership Magazine—Janu¬ 
ary, 1955.

NATURE LORE 


a • ■ 


/ 


At the Intermediate Level 



Elliott Larman, 

Nature Lore Counsellor, 

Camp B’Nai B’Rith , Montreal 


The intermediate age group is gen¬ 
erally considered to be between ages 
ten and twelve. These children de¬ 
mand a much more mature approach 
to nature lore than the Juniors, and 
they will closely watch the Juniors to 
see that their programme is not at the 
Junior level! Notwithstanding, they 
still love the nature walks and “col¬ 
lecting” trips, since these are appreci¬ 
ated by everyone from kindergarten to 
college age and beyond. 


Junior and Senior sections see Inter¬ 
mediates with their Star Gazer boxes, 
they become envious. The Nature Lore 
Counsellor should always bear in mind 
that every section knows what the 
other sections do. 

The Star Gazer is an attempt to get 
the children to know some of the more 
commonly observed constellations and 
the legends connected with them. This 
is the way it is made: 

An opening is cut out of one end ot 
a cardboard shoe box. This opening 
is covered with tissue paper. A peep 
hole is made in the exact centre ot the 
opposite end of the box by pushing the 
point of a pencil through it. Slits (for 
slides) are cut on both sides of the box 
about one-half inch from the open end. 

The Star Gazer is now made. 


The project most enthusiastically re¬ 
ceived by any group in my camping 
experience was the Star Gazer. Its 
only drawback is that it takes up so 
much time that it is not practical for 
an over-all camp programme. Unfor¬ 
tunately, the whole camp wants it, as 
a rule, for, whenever the children of 


Make slides from black craft paper 
on which the traced constellations are 
pricked out with a needle. The 
brighter the star, the bigger the hole 
pricked out. When pointed to the 
light, looking through the Star Gazer 
is like looking up at a constellation in 
the sky. 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1955 


25 



The five constellations best for use 
are the circumpolar constellations: 
Gassiopea, Cepheus, Draco, the Little 
Bear and the Great Bear. These are 
the subjects of interesting stories and 
are very simple to draw. Wonderful 
rainy day programme; usable souvenir 
of camping days. 

PLANTS 

Another favourite and effective pro¬ 
ject is the bean plant, the growing of 
which can explain many natural 
phenomena of plants. Insert a rolled 
up piece of blotting paper in a glass 
to cover the whole of its inside dia¬ 
meter. Pack lightly the inside area 
with sawdust, and soak it with water. 
Between the blotter and the side of the 
glass, three or four beans are placed 
equidistant from one another about 
two inches down from the top of the 
glass. The beans are left to germinate. 

There should be one plant for each 
camper; they should be watered each 
day and the stages of growth explained 
as often. When they have grown suf¬ 
ficiently, the plants can be exposed to 
various phenomena so that the 
trophisms of plants can be illustrated. 

One or two pl&nts should be placed 
in direct and constant sunlight; they 
will grow sturdily and well into 
healthy-looking bean plants until the 
food of the bean is used up. 

Other plants can be hung upside 
down from the ceiling so that campers 
can see the wonder of their growing in 
reverse, in relation to the earth. 

Show them, too, how plants turn 
towards sunlight. A paper bag, with 
but a small hole on one side, is placed 
about two or three plants. The plants 


will grow towards the hole, which is 
their only source of light. Care should 
be taken that the hole is placed so 
that sunlight will pass through it. 

The root systems and basic physi¬ 
ology of all plants can be explained 
using the bean plant as an example, 
since this seed contains so much stored 
food that it can develop to a great 
degree without need of being fed. 

TERRARIA 

A wooden box four feet square and 
approximately one foot high can be 
used as an excellent terrarium which 
can furnish projects, work and fun for 
a whole summer. It can be planted 
with various toadstools, puffballs, 
mosses, fungi and ferns, to mention 
only a few. Plants with complex root 
systems are not recommended. 

In its construction, the box should 
first be covered with two inches of 
sand, a few more inches of charcoal, 
and about five inches of rich black 
earth. The above-mentioned plants are 
easily transplanted. 

As the counsellor supervises the 
transplanting, the life cycle and funda¬ 
mental physiology of each plant can 
be explained. This will consume a 
great many interesting periods. 

To lend colour to the camp, the Ter¬ 
rarium can be decorated with painted 
rock. Campers could make a sign of 
suitable significance; “Cibbibba 
Jungle” was used last year at our 
Camp.

WHODUZIT? 


By W. E. (Ted) Yard 
Director , Camp Pinecrest 


This is the fourth in a series of 
“check-list” type articles. 

Most of us have, at one time or an¬ 
other, attempted to analyse the scope 
of various staff positions, and it has 
proven invariably to be a rewarding, 
though at times, laborious experience. 

Many camps use different titles for 
staff, and many who use similar titles, 
find quite logically that because of pe¬ 
culiarly individual characteristics and 
practices, they expect entirely different 
things from staff members who “nom¬ 
inally” fill the same position. 

We shall not suggest here that all 
staff should fit into “standardized” 
categories, since in the first place we 
suspect that such an endeavour would 
almost surely end in futility, and in the 
second place we are not convinced that 
“standardization” is the most impor¬ 
tant concern at the moment in this 
area. It does seem, however, that a 
careful thinking through of the detailed 
responsibilities of each position, de¬ 
veloped possibly to a written job analy¬ 
sis for that position in the individual 
camp, would be a worthwhile exercise 
and in keeping with our common con¬ 
cerns for good Personnel practices. 

CAMP MEDICAL STANDARDS 

The minimum standards for chil¬ 
drens’ camps developed by the Ontario 
Camping Association stipulate that 
every camp operated for more than 
two weeks and with more than 30 
campers must have in residence, either 
a graduate medical doctor or a regis¬ 
tered nurse. In the latter instance, 


each camp is required to arrange in 
writing, for a qualified medical doctor 
to be on call. In some instances camps 
engage a doctor and a nurse and in 
still other cases, two nurses are hired to 
assure the attendance in camp of a 
trained medical person at all times. 

It is a further requirement of the 
Standards Committee that each 
camper and staff member have a health 
examination within two weeks prior 
to going to camp. 

RESPONSIBILITIES OF MEDICAL 
STAFF 

1. Medical check-up of all campers on 
arrival, on departure, and in the 
case of long-term campers at some 
point in the middle of their camp 
period. 

2. Checking the health forms handed 
in by cabin counsellors daily, de¬ 
ciding which boys should be ex¬ 
amined at the morning “sick pa¬ 
rade” and conducting said 
examinations. 

3. Handling various situations which 
may occur in camp requiring medi¬ 
cal aid. 

4. Working with the Business Mana¬ 
ger to see that following matters 
are covered: — 

(a) Daily check and testing of 
water supply. 

(b) Weekly check of kitchen and 
cabin screening. 

(c) Daily check of out-houses and 
sanitation, including garbage 
and swill disposal. 


28 


Canadian Camping 



(d) Daily check of kitchen and 
dishwashing system for clean¬ 
liness. 

(e) Check regularly that laundry 
handled satisfactorily. 

5. Working with the Section 
Directors:— 

(a) To provide an initial introduc¬ 
tion to health standards when 
the boys arrive at camp. 

(b) To be sure that the daily cabin 
inspection for cleanliness is car¬ 
ried out adequately. 

(c) To act as resource persons for 
discussions related to medical 
field. 

6. Maintaining all first aid kits in good 
order. 

7. Caring for any child confined to the 
infirmary. 

8. Entering all treatments on campers’ 
cards and turning in a daily report 
to the Camp Director on the regu¬ 
lar forms. 

9. At the end of season: 

(a) Return all camp sheets and 
blankets. 

(b) Pack all medical supplies. 

(c) Prepare summary of treat¬ 
ments for summer. 

(d) Prepare inventory of all medi¬ 
cal goods in stock. 

(e) Prepare order for medical 
goods for following year.

me HAZARDS/ 


While none of us likes to think “it 
can happen in my camp”, fire could 
strike at any given moment, and with¬ 
out warning. In an effort to do away 
with the danger spots, a check list was 
prepared for the American Camping 
Association’s publication, Camping 
Magazine, and presented in their 1955 
Buying Guide. 

A portion of it is reprinted for your 
use this summer: 

AROUND THE CAMP AREA 

Have you removed all flammable 
rubbish and leaves from the area 
around buildings and tents? 

Are grass, brush and small trees cut 
or thinned out around camp build¬ 
ings? 

Is fire-fighting equipment within 
easy reach when trash, leaves, etc. 
are burned out-of-doors? 

Do you keep your storerooms and 
gargaes free from rubbish, oily 
rags, papers, etc.? 

Do you keep oil mops or paint rags 
in closed metal containers to guard 
against spontaneous ignition ? 

Are stoves always kept free of 
grease ? 


Do you have baking soda or salt 
handy in case of grease fires? 

Do you hang towels on special racks, 
never drying them on or near 
stoves ? 

Do you collect ashes in covered, hole- 
free metal containers, and dispose 
of them when properly cooled? 

Are ashes left to cool in a place far 
removed from the garbage area 
for dry paper? 

Do you keep matches in covered 
metal containers away from heat 
. . . and gnawing mice? 

Do you use only safety matches in 
camp? 

Do you have spark screens over all 
chimneys? 

Are all fireplaces equipped with ef¬ 
fective firescreens that fit each 
fireplace opening? 


FLAMMABLE LIQUIDS 

Do you start fires with paper and 
kindling only, never with flam¬ 
mable liquids?

RID YOUR PLACE 
" OF WEEDS AND PESTS 

Summer camps of all sorts can 
offer happier vacations by con¬ 
trolling weeds and pests with 

t; 

NIAGARA MATERIALS 

Mr. Art Ruttan will be contact¬ 
ing most Ontario operators dur¬ 
ing the season. For information 
write: 

NIAGARA BRAND 
SPRAY CO., LIMITED 

Burlington, Ontario 


Are kerosene lanterns always sus¬ 
pended from a secure hanger, 
never on the floor? 

Are supplies of fuel oil stored away 
from buildings, preferably in 
underground tanks? 

Are oils (kerosene and gasoline) 
handled only in the daylight and 
where spillage cannot be ignited? 

Do you use only approved hurricane- 
type lanterns with heavy bases to 
prevent tipping? 

..Do you store inflammable liquids 
of any quantity in a special ven¬ 
tilated building, under lock and 
key? 

WHAT ABOUT YOUR 
BUILDINGS? 

Are the roofs of your buildings non¬ 
combustible ? 

Have you used fire-proof roofing? 

Are roofs, gutters, chimneys and 
hoods above kitchen stoves cleaned 
and repaired before camp opens? 

Are floors directly under stoves and 
heaters protected by galvanized 
iron, concrete or brickwork? 

Have you eliminated all stovepipes 
which pass through closets or 
store-rooms? 

Are walls, rafters, ceilings and parti¬ 
tions protected from over-heating 
of stoves and pipes? 

FOR THE SMOKERS 

Do you insist that containers filled 
with sand take the place of ash 
trays in all smoking areas? 

Do you maintain restricted places 
for smoking ... for everyone? 


32 


Canadian Camping 




Do you insist, and repeat the instruc¬ 
tion from time to time, that all 
cigarette and cigar butts and pipes 
be carefully extinguished? 

Do you insist that matches be broken 
in two before being thrown away? 

ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT 

Are electric irons, toasters, and all 
electrical appliances used for cook¬ 
ing, equipped with metal stands or 
asbestos pads. 

If your electric iron or toaster stands 
on a shelf, is that shelf lined and 
padded with asbestos or metal 
sheeting? 

Do you place all electrical extension 
cords in the open, never under 
rugs or over metal hooks? 

Do you use standard fuses of proper 
capacity . . . 15’s where 15’s should 
be, 20*s where 20’s should be, etc.? 

Do you insist that a copper coin 
never be used with a blown-out 
fuse? (No insurance if this is 
found to be the cause of a fire!) 

Do you allow only qualified electri¬ 
cians to install your wiring and 
equipment ? 

ONE LAST WARNING 

Make sure that your garbage incin¬ 
erator is placed in a wide-open, tree¬ 
less area, that grass is cleared in a 
twelve-foot area (at least) around it, 
and that cardboard cartons or other 
rubbish is not allowed to remain near 
the outside of the incinerator.

FOLK SONGS OF CANADA by Edith 
Fulton Fowke and Richard Johnston 
with illustrations by Elizabeth Wilkes 
Hoey is published by the Waterloo Mu¬ 
sic Company Limited, Waterloo, On¬ 
tario. Price $4.95. 


sm A SOHO 

Of CANADA .., 

Dorothy M. Douglas 


The review of FOLK SONGS OF 
CANADA "by Fowke and Johnston 
which appeared in the February issue 
of “Canadian Camping” recommended 
this song collection for your camp 
library. Such a priceless book does in¬ 
deed belong on your music shelf, but 
the contents do not come to life or 
become part of the camp’s repertoire 
until a competent song leader intro¬ 
duce them to the camp. In these days 
of preparation for camp be sure this 
book in the hands of your music 
counsellor who will find that time spent 
in learning or refreshing the memory of 
these songs will bring rewards of sheer 
enjoyment to all. The following arc a 


few suggestions on how the songs might 
be introduced. 

Our Canadian Folk songs are filled 
with action, romance and adventure; 
many of them are about outdoor life. 
Their music is direct, simple, and much 
of it very rhythmic. They are “natu¬ 
rals” for group singing at camp. Folk 
songs do not require accompaniment, 
but if you wish to add harmonic flavour 
this book offers very suitable piano 
accompaniments and chord symbols for 
the guitar. In case anyone thinks that 
folk songs are deadwood, try Bon - 
homme, Bonhomme ( a superb cumu¬ 
lative song like Alouette, which is here 


34 


Canadian Camping 



too), The Day Columbus Landed Here, 
The Farmer’s Curst Wife (with a 
whistling line in every verse), or J7n- 
fortunate Miss Bailey for rollicking fun 
and humour. For poignant beauty The 
Morning Dew, The Blooming Bright 
Star of Belle Isle, or The False Young 
Man, are true gems. Here in print for 
the first time is Ontario’s nostalgic and 
lovely Land of the Silver Birch . 

Lots of the songs have a verse and 
chorus pattern, and many of them tell 
a story, which facts give us an idea. 
In almost every camp there are a num¬ 
ber of campers and counsellors who 
particularly enjoy singing, aren’t there? 
Gather them into an informal group 
who spend a little time learning your 
new songs before you introduce these 
to the larger camp group. (Here are 
your “pioneers”.) At your first session 
with the full camp, the campers could 
learn the chorus from this group; then 
you’ll have the group sing the verses 
while the campers join in the chorus. 
It won’t take many performances be¬ 
fore everyone will be chiming in on the 
verses too, especially in such songs as 
Jack was Every Inch a Sailor, Bonavist’ 
Harbour, Youpe Youpe, Lukey’s Boat 
(a dandy sailing song), Tse the Boy that 
Builds the Boat, Red River Valley. The 
largest number of our folk songs come 
from our French-Canadian ancestors. 
Campers would like to sing the choruses 
of many of these in the original French 
(every Canadian likes to say he can 
speak a little French) even if the verses 
follow the English translations offered 
here. 


Wouldn’t it be fun to present your 
“pioneers” from time to time as one, 
and then another type of early Cana¬ 
dian? Let us say the occasion could call 
for sailors from the Mari times, intro¬ 
ducing such sea songs as We’ll Rant 
and We’ll Roar, The Chesapeake and 
the Shannon, Squid Jiggin’ Ground, or 
Donkey Riding. How about the cour- 
eurs-de-bois with the rhythmic paddling, 
songs En Roulant Ma Boule, C’est 
L’Aviron, Youpe Youpe; or the lumber¬ 
men singing The Raftsmen, Lumber 
Camp Song, or Ye Maidens of Ontario. 
And a bunch of westerners could swing 
into Strawberry Roan, Old Grandma, 
Bury Me Out in the Lone Prairie . 

You might add one or two items of 
costume when your “pioneers” are sing¬ 
ing such special groups of songs. Infor¬ 
mal discussion about the historic back¬ 
ground helps too to get the feel of these 
songs—swapping ideas with the campers 
about the way of life, the dangers and 
excitements of the pioneer days. You’ll 
find that some of the songs beg for 
dramatic presentation on the camp 
stage or beside the fire. The campers or 
junior counsellors—closer to the history 
books than you or I—will contribute 
imaginative suggestions. 

It’s good to find that there are songs 
suitable for most age groups. Some 
might be a trifle “spicy” for some occa¬ 
sions. Maybe these, together with one 
or two gory ones and those that are 
really poignant, would intrigue the 
counsellors who like to gather round a 
piano after the day is over. 


Toronto , Canada 3 June , 1965 


35 



OUR WATERFRONT- 
LET’S MAKE IT FUN! 


Nancy Fairley 

Waterfront Director, 
Camp Tanamakoon 


The magic wand of teaching is fun! 
It is easy to learn things we enjoy 
doing, and conversely, teaching is 
easier if the pupil is having fun. 

Everyone accepts the fact that a 
Waterfront programme should provide 
knowledge. Assuming then that we 
have a good programme of basic in¬ 
struction, how can we make the learn¬ 
ing process fun? 

The success of any program will de¬ 
pend on our counsellors—their cheer¬ 
fulness, patience, imagination, creative¬ 
ness; their sincere care for each camper, 
and love for their work. 


First, let us look at our non-swim¬ 
mers. A frightened child will take 
longer to learn—therefore his first in¬ 
troduction to the water should be a 
happy experience, and this should start 
when he first sets foot on the dock. 
Meet him with a cheerful word; make 
him feel that learning to swim will be 
a barrel of fun, and continue this 
enthusiasm throughout each lesson. 

Make a game of the difficult spots, 
such as “adjustment to the water”— 
for example: 1 hold hands and play 
“follow-the-leader” into the water, 
with the instructor as the leader. 2 
Foot races; “Crows and Cranes”; “Fish 
in the Sea”; and other land games 
adapted to the water. 

As the lessons progress, so may the 
games. Once a camper can, in a man¬ 
ner of speaking, swim a short distance 
or across a pool, then simple relay 
races may be used. The games and 
races should never be beyond the 
ability of anyone in the group—but 


36 


Canadian Camping 




should involve skills the campers have 
already learnt, and can do reasonably 
well. Watch for any signs of tiredness 
or coldness. Bring the campers out of 
the water while they are still having 
fun, and they will be eager to return. 

Once a child has learned the basic 
steps of swimming, the problem is one 
of motivation. He is apt to be content 
with what he knows, and will be quite 
happy to play around in the depth of 
water he is accustomed to. His first 
excursion into deep water should be 
with a counsellor. Then, give him: 

1. Something special to work for—(a) 
a Red Cross programme where he 
may progress from a Junior through 
to a Senior Swimmer or (b) Royal 
Life Saving Society Classes, c. Rec¬ 
ognition within the camp—when he 
does achieve something, make sure 
others know about it. Give him the 
credit he deserves. 

2. Special events—(these will be taken 
up in more detail later on). 

3. Variations in the scheduling—so he 
will not be swimming with the same 
people, at the same time and at the 
same place, each day. (a) Swim¬ 
ming with his friends occasionally, 
or special swims in the cabin group 
with the counsellor is fun. (b) 
Change the locale of the lesson 
from time to time, that is, from one 
part of the dock to another, so he 
isn’t always climbing the same lad¬ 
der or gazing at the same knot-hole! 

4. Special equipment—such as Swim 
Fins and kick boards, are fun, when 
brought out in a play period or 
general swim, but no child should 
become dependent upon them alone 
for his fun. A word of warning— 
light floating objects should never 
be allowed outside an enclosed area 


—it takes only a light wind to carry 
them out into the lake. 

5. Organized demonstration pro¬ 
grammes by his more proficient 
friends, to spur him on. Give him 
a chance to be in a program too, to 
show what he has learned. 

For the advanced swimmer, the pro¬ 
gramme must be varied and challeng¬ 
ing. Don’t stop at the Senior Swimmer 
level, give your campers something 
further to work at: 

1. Special camp tests or awards— 
“advanced swimmer’’, “expert 
swimmer”, etc., with the emphasis 
on diving, speed, style; and syn¬ 
chronized swimming. 

2. Special interest groups or classes 
two or three times a week in: 

a. Diving; 

b. Style—elementary and advanced 
strokes; 

c. Speed — techniques of racing, 
starts and turns; 

d. Synchronized swimming— 
campers can make up routines 
and water ballets to perform for 
entire camp. 

3. Royal Life Saving Society Instruc¬ 
tor’s Certificate, Bronze Medallion or 

Award of Merit. 

4. Red Cross Leader’s Course—for 16 
and 17 year olds. 

5. Helping with beginners, under the 
supervision of a counsellor. 

6. Planning and helping with regattas, 
demonstrations and special events. 
(Campers bring a freshness to such

things, which is often lost by con¬ 
tinual planning by counsellors). 

These same fundamentals may be ap¬ 
plied to Canoeing and Sailing. The 
beginner should not be kept “paddling 
the dock” or learning sailing knots for 
hours on end. If he has the necessary 
swimming tests, get him out in the 
canoe or sail boat right away. 

“Taxi Rides”—where the beginners 
are invited by the counsellors, C.I.T.’s, 
or experienced campers, are a good 
way to interest the younger campers. 

For the average sailor or canoeist, 
the need for motivation again arises: 

1. Canoe Parades or Paddle Pasts 
(with the Director taking the 
salute). 

2. Canoeing Demonstrations by 
campers, of strokes, rescues and 
special skills. 

3. Impromptu sailing races, when the 
wind is good. 

4. “Sailing lunches”—campers take a 
picnic lunch and go off for two or 
three hours of sailing (for those 
swimmers who rate.) 

5. “Vagabond Days”—all day expedi¬ 
tions by Canoe. 

The advanced or senior campers 
may have the fun of organizing a Yacht 
Club, with its executive, sailing com¬ 
mittee (to arrange all the races), en¬ 
tertainment committee, and so on. 
(Membership in the Yacht Club should 
be open to any camper who is inter¬ 
ested in Sailing, and who has the neces¬ 
sary swimming qualifications). 

Fun in the Group 

Regattas and Special Events should 
be held from time to time, but not too 
often, or the novetly and spontaneous 



38 


Canadian Camping 



fun of them will wear off. Regattas— 
may be planned or impromptu (to the 
campers); they may take a whole day, 
or just a morning or afternoon. They 
may be a combined effort of the Swim¬ 
ming, Canoeing and Sailing depart¬ 
ments, or they may be separate small 
affairs within each activity. 

But whatever the type, length or 
size of a Regatta or Waterfront event, 
the following points should be kept in 
mind: 

1. It is extremely important that every 
detail is planned ahead of time. The 
starters, judges, announcers, run¬ 
ners, etc. should know exactly what 
their duties are and where they are 
to be. All equipment should be on 
hand. 

2. Each camper should be in an equal 
number of events. 

3. No camper should compete in one 
race following another. 

4. The events should be based on the 
ability and ages of the different 
groups. 

It has been my experience that Team 
competiiton rather than individual 
competition is more fun, and is of 
greater benefit to the campers. The 
teams, chosen at the beginning of 
camp, should be of equal strength—i. e. 
there should be the same number of 
advanced swimmers and stern paddlers 
on each.

Stunts or humourous skits put on by 
counsellors, C.I.T.’s or older campers 
are always an added and well received 
attraction of any Regatta. The events 
should include humourous races— 
such as. Swimming “Pyjama”, “News¬ 
paper”, “Candle”, “Potato” or “Bal¬ 
loon” Races; or Canoeing “Obstacle”, 
“Crab”, “Wash basin” (make sure the 
basins are tied to the gunwhales), of 
“Broom” races, as well as straight free¬ 
style or “crew of four”. 

On looking back, we note that—Be¬ 
ginners in any activity need to over¬ 
come fear; the next group need 
motivation; and the more advanced 
campers need to be given responsibility. 
The password to progress all along the 
way is fun—let’s give it to them!

MARK TRAIL’S BOOK OF 
NORTH AMERICAN MAMMALS. 

Ed. Dodd. 

For years we have followed Mark 
Trail, one of the best comic strips ever, 
and often felt he should do a book on 
naturelore; which he did. Ed. Dodd, 
Mark’s creator, couldn’t have made a 
better choice than the larger animals 
of our continent. His realistic pen 
drawings show the animals in natural 
surroundings, completely un-posed, and 
his concise copy highlights the inter¬ 
esting habits and characteristics of 
those creatures readily recognized, as 
well as many j we might never see. 
Pocket size, this book is a welcome aid 
to the study of wild life, and belongs as 
much on the home shelf as at camp. 
$2.35. McClelland & Stewart, Lim¬ 
ited, Toronto 16. 

WOODSMOKE AT TWILIGHT. 

A. Norman McMillan. 

Although this series of stories was 
dedicated to Cubs and Scouts, there 
is no reason why they cannot be studied 
by any counsellor anywhere, to be 
used as the basis of campfire talks or 
for reading to younger boys or girls. 
There is inspiration in each story, as it 
emphasizes the strength and weaknesses 
of almost every type of person one 
meets, especially in the camp setting. 
The author shows wisdom in the man¬ 


ner of handling each problem as it 
arises, and writes of each one in a 
style easy to read and absorb. $1.00. 
G. R. Welch Co., Ltd., Toronto. 


INTEREST GROUP BOOKLETS. 

To assist such group leaders in 
C.G.I.T. work, the Canadian Council 
of Churches, Department of Christian 
Education, published a ..series of book¬ 
lets, one on each of the following sub¬ 
jects: NATURELORE, CAMP- 
CRAFT, ART, PUPPETRY, 
CRAFTS, each discussed by authors 
distinguished in each field: Mrs. R. A. 
Colpits, Bridgetown, N.S.; Miss Helen 
Beals, Department of Art, Acadia Uni¬ 
versity, Wolfville, N.S.; Miss Ada 
Adams, National Secretary for Chil¬ 
dren’s Work of., the Presbyterian 
Church in Canada; Miss Jessie Scott, 
of the National C.G.I.T. Camp Com¬ 
mittee; Miss Margaret Govan, Direc¬ 
tor, Camp Onawa. Since these are 
small books, they are, necessarily con¬ 
cise and “meaty”, and could easily be 
the key assistants to successful pro¬ 
grammes in any of the above fields. 25c 
each, ordered through the Provincial 
Christian Education Supply Depots.

THE WEB OF LIFE. 

John H. Storer. 

To explain to the average reader 
some of the fundamentals of ecology 
(the study of how one living thing 
affects another) Mr. Storer wrote this 
book in the simplest possible fashion. 
The Web of Life shows how the natural 
world operates, without benefit of man 
and machines; it shows the natural 
community in action, with all its parts 
functioning. To those interested in 
conservation and natural history, in 
the wise use of soil, water, forests and 
wildlife, this book is the Open Door. 
$3.25. Thomas Nelson & Sons (Can¬ 
ada) Limited, Toronto. 

WAGONS WEST. 

John Craig. 

The story of Dick Brandon and his 
family winding their way along the 
exciting and difficult wagon trail half 
way across the continent of America 
in 1842, brings as true a picture of his¬ 
tory as it does excitement to younger 
readers. Author John Craig, a student 
of history, Ontario born and Winnipeg 
bred, has gathered much in the way 
of first-hand knowledge of the old 
West. Actually this story covers the 
Oregon Trail, its thrills, its dangers 
and the final achievement of new settle¬ 
ments in a new world. An excellent 
book for the campers’ bookshelf. $2.25. 
J. M. Dent & Sons (Canada), Limited, 
Toronto 5.

was that everybody on the staff—

i'abin / iHiiixrlhtrx 

The counsellor is one of the most 
important persons on your camp stall. 
In connection with a city, we know 
that the mayor is a very important 
personage but it’s the parents who 
have the most influence upon the lives 
of boys and girls. The counsellors are 
like the parents. Therefore, your coun¬ 
sellor should be the best-trained. II 
your leaders are paid, he should be 
the highest paid. 

The most important things in your 
camp happen to the campers in the 
small cabin groups. 

Don’t have counsellors who are too 
young. If you’ve got to have a young 
counsellor put him in with an older 
cabin group. They’re better able to 
protect themselves. The younger the 
camper, the better the leader he needs. 

Your best counsellors will have 
maturity, training, practical experi¬ 
ence. Look out for the leader who has 
merely theoretical book learning. Re¬ 
member the mother who brought up 
her child by the book—the child finally 
died of a misprint. 

The counsellor’s lot is a hard, hard 
lot. For instance, the campers may be

a bore to him. A bore is someone who 
deprives you of your solitude without 
providing you with company. 

Just look at him, the counsellor sur¬ 
rounded by a bunch of junior kids. 
One junior holds on his leg. Another 
junior is astride his back. And two 
more have a hold on his sweat shirt. 
The sweat shirt is pulled out of shape 
giving the counsellor that Dior look. 

And what is the poor counsellor 
thinking? Probably something like 
this—he could be at the cottage with 
his wife. When they first talked over 
the idea of camp, she had said, “It 
will be a change for you, darling.” The 
counsellor might have gone to Banff as 
a waitress or a caddie. Maybe he’s a 
cool cat and could be at home listen¬ 
ing to those Dave Brubeck records. Or 
maybe he’s frustrated because the chief 
found out about his moon light canoe 
excursion with that cute little blonde 
riding instructress. There are things 
more important than chasing girls. 
Catching them is important, too. 

On the other hand, counsellors can 
form a pressure labor group . . . days 
off . . . moonlight dips . . . use of sail¬ 
boats, etc. . . . pantry privileges . . . 
midnight snacks . . . unlimited curfew 
. . . weekend dance in the dining hall. 

. . . Go to bed when the campers do? 
“Listen, egghead, didn’t you read the 
fine print in my contract?” The di¬ 
rector’s lot is a hard, hard lot!

TAPS . . . 


Day is done, 

Gone the sun, 

Clear, through the gathering dusk, a bugle sounds, 

In quick response the campers turn from play; 

While through the silent hills the call resounds, 

They stand erect to honor close of day. 

From the lake, 

From the hills, 

From the sky. 

From western skies the colors slowly die, 

The stars above the pines their watches keep. 

Another joyous day goes swiftly by, 

Another night bestows her gift of sleep. 

All is well, 

Safely rest, 

A treasure-trove, life in the open, brings, 

Of magic gifts to hold for years to be. 

Adventure, laughter, friends—all goodly things, 

And lessons learned from flower, bird and tree. 

A sense of genuine pride in work well done, 

A strength of body and a glowing tan. 

Joy of achievement in a skill new-won, 

Assurance “all is well” in life’s great plan. 

God is nigh. 

As ’neath the stars the echoes softly fade, 

An over-ruling sense of peace is there. 

Since “God is nigh”, no need to be afraid. 

He hears the faintest whisper of a prayer. 

From, “Under Open Skies ”—Excerpts from Chapel Talks and Poetry— 

By Mary S. Edgar 


To be published by Clarke Irwin & Co. Ltd. in the autumn of 1955. 


Toronto, Canada , June, 1955

STOP PRESS NEWS! 


From the Convention Manager of 
the Royal York Hotel, Mr. G. R. 
Street, through the Convention Man¬ 
ager of the Ontario Camping Associa¬ 
tion, Mr. Clifford Labbett, comes 
news of the 1956 annual gathering of 
camping people. The Camping Con¬ 
vention is slated for March 1, 2 and 
3, 1956, at the Royal York Hotel, 
and various members of the Commit¬ 
tee are at work now mapping the 
course our meetings are to take. 

We have been warned . . . and 
we pass it on to all our readers . . . 
that space at the hotel, for those 
who wish to stay there, will not be 
very plentiful, since another large con¬ 
ference will be in progress at the 
same time. So, if you plan to stay at 
the Royal York, outline your trip now 
as much as possible, and make your 
reservations EARLY!
